newsitem.title: USA: Coastal Physician learns fate next month.
newsitem.headline: Coastal Physician learns fate next month.

text.p: Coastal Physician Group Inc investors voted Friday on whether the board of directors should stick with plans for the struggling physician-management company's recovery while it shops for a buyer. They also voted on whether a dissident board member will take over the company.
But officials will not know the outcome until next month.
Voting was extended until 1700 EDT Friday due to Coastal Physician's proxy fight with recently ousted chief executive Steven Scott, founder and owner of 30 percent of the company.

Scott remains on the nine-members board of directors, of which three members were up for re-election. But in a proxy statement of his own, Scott offered a slate of three directors that would allow him to regain control of the company even if just two win election.

The result of the vote was due Oct. 10, Coastal Physician Chairman Jacque Sokolov told investors during the company's annual meeting, which he brought to order by announcing it was "not a typical shareholders meeting" and appealed for all to be "professional."

But when he told investors polls would remain open, Scott objected, raising a brief ruckus. Afterwards he said: "I didn't want the rest of day to keep this thing divided. The meeting's over, the ballots are in, let's stop. Why are we going to continue this on."
But Chief Executive Joseph Piemont said voting was extended in efforts to avoid shareholder confusion as a result of the various proxy materials distributed.
"This is a highly contested matter and we think it is going to be extremely close," the chief executive said.
Shareholders were reticent at the meeting, not questioning the proposals before them or business in general despite the widely publicized feud between Scott and board members.
The spat ensued after Scott led Coastal Physician on an acquisition spree in 1993, that left the company mired in debt.
Coastal Physician's net losses soared to $24.9 million, or $1.04 in the second quarter compared with a loss of $10.5 million, or $0.44, in the same year-ago period.
Its 1996, second-quarter losses were attributed to contract attrition and lower new business development during the second half of 1995, in the hospital-based contract services division.

It also cited lower collections per patient visit in the billing and accounts receivable management services division, increased investments associated with growth in the company's health plans, and increased expenses in information technology.
In May, the board of directors put Scott on "sabbatical" and replaced him with Piemont who was general counsel.
Since then Price Waterhouse's Business Turnaround Services and Smith Barney Inc. has been hired to help restore profits and advise in evaluating on the possible sale of the entire company.
Sokolov and Piemont told investors the turnaround was realistic and responsible although a suitor was being sought.
"We are not going to throw this company on the market without trying to improve it .... It would be wrong to quit on Coastal," Piemont said.
Shares were up 1/4 at 6-1/4.
But Scott, who has amassed 30 percent of the 23.7 million shares outstanding since he founded the company in 1977, supports selling the company, responded it was too late for a turnaround.
"It's just not enough sand left in the hourglass, and there are buyers," he said.
